source_text: Hoc ergo arbitrium liberum, propter quod solum nos manifestari ante tribunal Christi, Magister Gentium scribit, ut reportet unusquisque propria corporis prout gessit, sive bonum, sive malum [n247] , sicut Catholici quidem confitentur; ita vos non solum cum Manichaeo, sed etiam cum Ioviniano, quem nobis audes impingere, diverso quidem genere, sed impietate simili denegatis. Quod ut planius fiat, divisionum adhibeatur examen. Nos dicimus peccato hominis, non naturae statum mutari, sed meriti qualitatem; id est, et in peccante hanc esse liberi arbitrii naturam, per quam potest a peccato desinere, quae fuit in eo ut posset a iustitia deviare.
pass_a_gloss: This free choice therefore, on account of which alone the Teacher of the Nations writes that we are to be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ, that each one may carry back the proper things of the body as he has carried, whether good or evil, as Catholics indeed confess; so you not only with the Manichaean, but also with Jovinian, whom you dare to pin on us, by a diverse kind indeed, but with a similar impiety deny. Which that it may become plainer, let an examination of divisions be applied. We say that by the sin of a human, not the status of nature is changed, but the quality of desert; that is, even in the one sinning this is the nature of free choice, through which he can cease from sin, which was in him that he could deviate from justice.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil

pass_b_english: It is solely because of this free choice, the Teacher of the Nations writes, that we must be revealed before Christ's judgment seat, so that each may receive what belongs to the body's deeds, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5:10). Catholics acknowledge this free choice, but you deny it, not only with Mani but also with Jovinian, whom you dare to pin on us. Your denial takes a different form but involves similar impiety. To make this clearer, let us examine the distinctions. We say that a person's sin changes not the state of nature but the character of what the person deserves. That is, in the sinner the nature of free choice remains the same: through it he can cease from sin, just as through it he was able to depart from righteousness.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
